messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 42

He is a seventy-nine-year-old man, broad-shouldered and slow-moving, who has worked in the same warehouse for forty-two years. The other men call him “Old Man,” but they step aside when he lifts a pallet. He speaks little, and when he does, it is about the work—where the boxes go, which machine needs oil. He keeps his head down, his hands busy, and his back to the wall. In the break room, he sits alone by the door, facing the room, watching. No one notices that he never lets anyone stand behind him.

It was his father’s hand that he still sees. Not the fist, but the open palm coming down on his mother’s face, again and again, in the cramped kitchen of their flat in a West African city. He was five, maybe six. He remembers the smell of palm oil and the sound of her teeth hitting the floor. He remembers his own body frozen behind the doorframe, his throat closed, his bladder letting go. He remembers the silence afterward, his mother washing the blood from her mouth, his father sitting at the table as if nothing had happened. No one spoke of it. Not that night, not ever.

He learned early that the world was not safe—that the people who were supposed to protect you could hurt you, and that there was nothing you could do. So he learned to be small, to be still, to watch his father’s moods like a weatherman watches a storm. He never cried. He never told. At school, he was called “the ghost” because he was so quiet. At night, he lay awake listening for the sound of footsteps, for the crash of a chair.

He left home at sixteen, worked in mines, then moved to this country, got a job in the warehouse, and married a woman who was patient and kind. But he could not let her close. He could not sleep beside her without jerking awake. He could not hear a sudden loud noise—a dropped pan, a slammed door—without his heart slamming inside his ribs. He would check every lock three times before bed. He would pace the house when she was gone, certain that something terrible had happened to her. She tried to hold him; he went rigid. She cried; he felt nothing but a hollow ache. After fifteen years, she left. He understood. He knew he was “hard to love.” He did not fight it.

In the warehouse, he found his rhythm. The repetition of the work—stacking, wrapping, loading—keeps the past from rising. But it always rises. The clatter of a dropped crate sends him into the past; he sees his father’s hand, his mother’s blood. He freezes for a second, then moves again, hiding the tremor in his hands. He never talks about the old country. When a younger worker asks about his scarred hands, he shrugs. He does not say that the scars came from a moment he does not remember—a broken bottle, a fight he walked into blind.

Now, at seventy-nine, his body is slowing down, but his mind is still fast with fear. He drives home the same route every day, avoiding the street with the bar where men sometimes argue. He eats alone and watches television, but he does not watch movies with violence. He flinches at the sound of a door slamming in the apartment next door. He has dreams, bad ones, of the kitchen, of being trapped, of not being able to scream. He wakes at three in the morning, every night, and waits for dawn.

He came to therapy because his doctor told him his blood pressure was dangerous. The doctor asked about stress. He said nothing for a long time. Then he said, “I saw things. When I was small.” That was all. But he came back the next week, and the week after. He sits in the chair with his hands on his knees, ready to stand, watching the door. He is still watching. He is still waiting.
